text: Time to build a QUBO matrix yourself, from a graph you haven't seen solved yet, and confirm the result by brute force. This lab closes out Chapter 1 by making the full pipeline -- graph, to per-edge terms, to Q matrix, to evaluated cost -- something you've done with your own hands.

Here's a new 5-node graph: nodes 0 through 4, with edges 0-1, 0-2, 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, and 3-4 -- picture a tight triangle on nodes 0, 1, 2, with nodes 3 and 4 bridging off it. Building the Q matrix edge by edge, every node accumulates a diagonal entry equal to negative 1 times its degree, and every edge contributes plus 2 to its off-diagonal entry. Node 1 touches 3 edges, so Q_11 equals negative 3; nodes 3 and 4 each touch 2 edges, giving Q_33 and Q_44 both negative 2.

Evaluating x equals 1,1,0,0,1 using the matrix form gives f equals negative 2 minus 3 minus 2 plus 2, equal to negative 5. Cross-checking against the direct cut count takes real care: re-examine every edge against the actual assignment values, and you'll find edges 0-2, 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, and 3-4 are all cut -- only edge 0-1 is not. That's 5 cut edges, and negative 5 matches the matrix computation exactly. The lesson: always recount every edge before trusting a mismatch.

Checking all 32 possible assignments directly, the true maximum cut on this graph is 5 out of 6 edges -- one edge is always left uncut, because the triangle formed by nodes 0, 1, and 2 can never have all three of its edges cut simultaneously. Four assignments achieve this optimum of 5, including the one just verified and its mirror image, where every 0 and 1 are swapped.

This exact three-step process -- build Q from the edge list, evaluate a candidate by hand, brute-force confirm on a small instance -- is precisely what you'll repeat with portfolio QUBOs in Lesson 15, and what you'll feed into a real QAOA circuit starting in Chapter 2, which opens with the circuit structure that actually runs these Ising Hamiltonians on quantum hardware.
